title: UI Cross-Cutting Scenarios (Compose + Views + Rendering)
scopeHtml: Scenario-heavy bank combining Compose, RecyclerView, rendering and migration. Versions cited: strong skipping is on by default from Kotlin 2.0.20 (compose compiler plugin); edge-to-edge is enforced on Android 15+ for targetSdk 35; anything else version-specific is marked "verify".

questions.promptHtml: How do you find out which composables are recomposing too often, and how do you read the numbers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who guess at performance from people who measure first.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I open Layout Inspector on a debuggable build, enable "Show recomposition counts", then perform the interaction (scroll, type) and watch two columns: recomposition count and skip count. A composable with a high recomposition count and a skip count near zero is recomposing with changed inputs every time; a high skip count is healthy. I then reset counts, repeat one gesture, and compare, so I measure per interaction and not since launch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose tracks per-composable counts of how many times its group executed (recomposed) versus how many times the compiler-generated check decided to skip it because parameters were equal. Layout Inspector (Android Studio, device/emulator, debuggable app) renders these as columns in the component tree.

Node            Recomp   Skipped
Feed                1        0
 FeedItem(id=7)    94        0   <-- every scroll frame: suspicious
 FeedItem(id=8)     1       93   <-- healthy: skipped

Reading rules:

  • Reset counts before each test; absolute numbers since launch mean nothing.
  • Expected: leaf composables that read changing state recompose; parents should not.
  • A parent with high count and children with high skip means the parent reads state too high (the children are fine, the scope boundary is wrong).
  • Debug builds exaggerate cost, but counts are valid in debug; timings are not. Counts tell you who recomposes, not why. For why, use compiler reports (unstable params) and state-read audit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Narrow the read so only the badge recomposes, not the whole header.
@Composable
fun Header(count: () -> Int) {          // lambda defers the read
    Text("Inbox")
    Badge { Text("${count()}") }        // read happens inside Badge's scope
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Judging by absolute counts after a long session.
  • Treating any recomposition as a bug; recomposition is cheap when inputs actually changed.
  • Profiling timings in a debug build.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would a composable recompose but never skip? → Its parameters change every time (new list instance, unstable param with strong skipping off) or it reads state directly.
  2. Does a skip count mean no work happened? → The body did not run; the parent's lambda still ran.
  3. How do you do this in CI? → Compiler metrics for stability plus Macrobenchmark/JankStats for outcomes; Layout Inspector is manual.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Layout Inspector". Senior: resets counts per gesture, correlates with compiler reports, distinguishes the read site from the symptom site, and confirms with a trace in a release-like build.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team chased a "slow feed" for a week in debug timings; the counts showed the header recomposing 60 times per scroll because it read the scroll offset directly.

questions.contextHtml:
A cart screen: tapping "Add" appends an item but the list on screen does not update until the user rotates the phone. QA files it as "intermittent". Code:

@Composable
fun Cart(vm: CartViewModel = viewModel()) {
    val items = remember { mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<Item>()) }
    Column {
        Button(onClick = { items.value.add(Item("x")) }) { Text("Add") }
        items.value.forEach { Text(it.name) }
    }
}

Red herring: the ViewModel is unused and someone suspects viewModel().
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose is buggy, call notifyDataSetChanged equivalent" or wrapping in LaunchedEffect. Misses that state holds a reference, not the contents.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce every time, or only first tap? (Rotation re-runs remember? No, rotation recreates the Activity so state resets and the list is rebuilt, which is why rotate "fixes" it.) Is the VM meant to own the cart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; hotfix is replacing the list instance on each add.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) in-place mutation of a plain MutableList inside MutableState (snapshot never sees a write); (b) missing state hoist; (c) viewModel() problem (red herring, unused).
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector shows zero recompositions on tap; add a log in the body to confirm.
  5. Root cause: MutableState notifies only when value is assigned a different object (structural equality by default). add() mutates the same ArrayList and the state object never records a write, so no scope is invalidated.
  6. Fix: Short term items.value = items.value + Item("x"). Long term use mutableStateListOf<Item>(), or better hoist an immutable StateFlow<List<Item>> in the VM and collectAsStateWithLifecycle().
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no MutableList inside mutableStateOf; state types expose read-only List.
  8. Trade-offs: mutableStateListOf is observable per-element but not thread-agnostic for huge lists; I would NOT call LaunchedEffect or force recomposition manually.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does items.value = items.value not work? → Same instance, equal by equals, so the neutral-equality policy skips the write.
  • What if the list has 10k items and you copy on every add? → O(n) copy per add; use persistentListOf or paging; measure first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout bug lived for two releases because rotation "healed" it; the team's fix was a global ImmutableList wrapper type enforced by a custom lint rule.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the framework or forces recomposition.
  • Hire: identifies in-place mutation, fixes with new instance or mutableStateListOf.
  • Strong hire: explains write tracking, equality policy, rotation red herring, and hoists to VM with immutable state.

questions.contextHtml:
Shopping feed, 2M DAU, mid-range devices. After adding a collapsing toolbar, p95 frame time on scroll went from 9 ms to 19 ms and jank rate (JankStats) from 2% to 11%. Layout Inspector: the entire FeedScreen shows ~60 recompositions per second of scroll, every card included. Code:

@Composable
fun FeedScreen(items: List<Product>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val offset = listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset   // read here
    Column {
        Toolbar(alpha = 1f - (offset / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f))
        LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(items, key = { it.id }) { ProductCard(it) } }
    }
}

Red herring: the team suspects Coil image loading.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without redesigning the screen.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add remember everywhere" or "use fewer images". Doesn't locate the state read.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Release or debug measurements? Did jank begin exactly with the toolbar commit? Does the effect also happen with images disabled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag the collapsing effect off if the release is hot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) scroll offset read in FeedScreen body so the whole scope recomposes each frame; (2) unstable Product blocking card skipping; (3) image decoding; (4) lazy item without contentType.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recomposition counts (screen is the hot node, cards recompose too); compiler report for Product; trace with image loading stubbed.
  5. Root cause: The read of firstVisibleItemScrollOffset happens during composition of FeedScreen, so the scope subscribes to a value that changes every scroll frame. Strong skipping may skip cards with equal params, but FeedScreen, Column and Toolbar re-execute, and unstable Product cards (if skipping is off) recompose too.
  6. Fix: Short term defer the read to a later phase.
Toolbar(alphaProvider = { 1f - (listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f) })

@Composable
fun Toolbar(alphaProvider: () -> Float) {
    Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = alphaProvider() })   // read in draw/layer phase
}

Long term, expose the collapse fraction as a state holder used only in layer/layout lambdas. 7. Prevention: Review rule "scroll/animation state is read in lambdas"; JankStats threshold in a Macrobenchmark gate. 8. Trade-offs: derivedStateOf would reduce frequency but the value is continuous, so not helpful; I would NOT debounce the scroll value, which makes the toolbar laggy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does graphicsLayer {} help? → The lambda is read in the draw/layer phase, skipping composition and layout.
  • What if the offset drives layout (toolbar height)? → Read inside Modifier.layout/offset { } lambda: layout phase only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A parallax header cost a team 8 ms per frame; moving a single read into graphicsLayer returned the frame to budget with a 4-line diff.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks images or adds remember.
  • Hire: finds the high read, defers via lambda/graphicsLayer.
  • Strong hire: names phases, verifies with counts and trace, adds a regression gate.

questions.contextHtml:
Search screen on a 4 GB low-end device (about 30% of DAU). Typing into the search box drops characters and feels delayed ~250 ms. Logs: Skipped 41 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread. Code:

val query by vm.query.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
TextField(value = query, onValueChange = { vm.onQuery(it) })   // VM: viewModelScope.launch { _query.value = it }

VM onQuery also filters 8k in-memory products with a regex and sorts them synchronously before updating _query. Red herring: keyboard app is blamed.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the field lag and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Debounce the input." Debouncing hides lag by dropping the text state itself.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does the text state live and on which thread is onQuery executed? Does lag exist with search disabled? Which devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable live filtering, search on submit, until the fix ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) heavy work on Main before the text state updates; (2) async state round-trip (value updated after coroutine dispatch) causing cursor jumps; (3) results list recomposing on each key; (4) IME.
  4. How I'd verify each: System trace around onQuery; Trace.beginSection markers; Layout Inspector counts on result list during typing.
  5. Root cause: TextField is a controlled input: the value must be updated synchronously in the same frame as the edit. Here the committed state is written after expensive Main-thread work, so each keystroke blocks a frame, and an asynchronous write also races with the IME's composing region.
  6. Fix: Keep the text in local state updated synchronously; do search work off-main.
var text by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
TextField(value = text, onValueChange = { text = it; vm.search(it) })

// VM
private val q = MutableStateFlow("")
val results = q.debounce(150).distinctUntilChanged()
    .mapLatest { filterAndSort(it) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

Also make the results list stable-keyed, with contentType. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark typing test with FrameTimingMetric; rule: no CPU work in onValueChange. 8. Trade-offs: Debouncing the query is fine; debouncing the displayed text is not. I would NOT move the text itself into a Flow (creates the async-write race).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the VM own the text? → For a short synchronous field, a local state or a state holder updated synchronously is fine; UDF to VM is possible if it is synchronous (see A4).
  • TextFieldState (BasicTextField state API)? → Newer stable-ish API removes this race; verify current stability for your Compose version.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search bar felt "laggy only on cheap phones" because a sort ran before the state write; moving the write first cut keystroke latency from ~250 ms to one frame.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debounces the text.
  • Hire: synchronous text state, heavy work off main.
  • Strong hire: explains the controlled-input contract, IME composing race, adds benchmark.

questions.contextHtml:
A news list where each card has an "expanded" toggle. Bugs reported: (1) after scrolling an expanded card off-screen and back it collapses; (2) after pull-to-refresh, a different card appears expanded; (3) after rotation, scroll position resets to top. Code:

LazyColumn {
    items(news) { n ->                       // no key
        var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
        NewsCard(n, expanded) { expanded = !expanded }
    }
}

and val listState = LazyListState() created in the composable body without remember. Red herring: "LazyColumn recycles views like RecyclerView and loses state".
questions.promptHtml: Explain each symptom and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds rememberSaveable everywhere and calls it done; cannot explain symptom 2.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is id stable across refresh? Is the expanded flag UI-only or business data? Process-death requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for crash; ship fix next release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) remember is dropped when an item leaves composition (lazy layouts dispose off-screen items beyond the prefetch/retention window); (2) positional identity, no key, so slot 3 keeps its state when the data under it changes; (3) LazyListState recreated each recomposition and not saveable.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in DisposableEffect to see disposal; refresh with reordered data; check rememberLazyListState usage.
  5. Root cause: remember state lives in the slot table tied to the composition group. Lazy items outside the viewport are disposed, and without key state is keyed by index.
  6. Fix:
val listState = rememberLazyListState()   // saveable by default
LazyColumn(state = listState) {
    items(news, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "news" }) { n ->
        var expanded by rememberSaveable(n.id) { mutableStateOf(false) }
        NewsCard(n, expanded) { expanded = !expanded }
    }
}

Long term, hoist expanded ids into a Set<Long> in a state holder when it influences other UI. 7. Prevention: Lint/review: lazy items always has key; key must be Bundle-saveable (Long/String). 8. Trade-offs: rememberSaveable per item adds saved-state entries (Bundle size, see Q381); I would NOT key by index or by object hash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does key guarantee retention off-screen? → It gives identity and lets rememberSaveable restore; plain remember is still disposed.
  • Duplicate keys? → Runtime crash ("Key ... was already used"); ensure uniqueness.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random card expanded after refresh" bug turned out to be index identity with a server list that prepended items.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames recycling.
  • Hire: adds keys and rememberSaveable.
  • Strong hire: explains disposal vs identity, saveable key constraints, hoists when shared.

questions.contextHtml:
A splash/ onboarding screen should navigate after a 3-second timer. After a recent refactor, QA reports it sometimes navigates to the previous screen's destination, and analytics shows onTimeout firing with an outdated user id. Code:

@Composable
fun Onboarding(userId: String, onTimeout: (String) -> Unit) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(3_000)
        onTimeout(userId)
    }
}

userId changes from "" to the real id after a profile fetch around t=1 s. Red herring: delay is blamed as being imprecise.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the id stale and what are the correct fixes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Changes the key to userId, which restarts the timer (new bug) and calls it done.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should the timer restart when userId changes, or just use the latest value? Is onTimeout a lambda created inline (changes each recomposition)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; fix before release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) effect captured first-composition userId and onTimeout because the key never changes; (2) recomposition ordering; (3) coroutine timing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the captured value at launch vs at call; change userId mid-delay in a test with mainClock.
  5. Root cause: A LaunchedEffect body is a closure created when the effect starts; with Unit as key it runs once and keeps the values captured at that moment.
  6. Fix: Use rememberUpdatedState when the effect should not restart but needs the latest value.
val currentId by rememberUpdatedState(userId)
val currentCb by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)
LaunchedEffect(Unit) { delay(3_000); currentCb(currentId) }

Use LaunchedEffect(userId) only if restarting the timer is the desired semantics. 7. Prevention: Review rule: every value read inside an effect is either a key or wrapped in rememberUpdatedState; lint rule exists for some cases (verify). 8. Trade-offs: rememberUpdatedState reads the latest at read time (could differ from value at decision time); I would NOT silence by moving logic into composition.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not read userId directly, it is a parameter? → The parameter binding is captured by value in the closure at launch.
  • State object instead? → Passing State<String> also works; reading .value inside gives latest.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "welcome back" tracking event attributed purchases to the wrong account for weeks due to a captured parameter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes keys blindly.
  • Hire: rememberUpdatedState.
  • Strong hire: contrasts restart vs latest-value semantics and explains closure capture.

questions.contextHtml:
A legacy orders list (RecyclerView + ListAdapter, ~300 rows). After a refactor, when the order status changes via push, the whole list flickers and the item animator plays fade-out/fade-in on every row; scroll position jumps. Crash-free and ANR rates unaffected. Diff callback:

object Diff : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Order>() {
    override fun areItemsTheSame(a: Order, b: Order) = a == b
    override fun areContentsTheSame(a: Order, b: Order) = a.id == b.id
}

Red herring: a recent RecyclerView library bump.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the diff and how does it cause both symptoms?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call notifyDataSetChanged" or disable animations, which treats the symptom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Order a data class? Is a new list submitted by submitList? Is setHasStableIds used?
  2. Immediate mitigation: itemAnimator = null temporarily if the UX is hot; real fix is the callback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) areItemsTheSame compares whole objects (identity of item = equality of content), so any changed row is treated as removed+inserted; (2) areContentsTheSame compares id only, so real changes never rebind (stale rows); (3) library bump.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test the callback; log onBindViewHolder and animator events; check payload.
  5. Root cause: The two methods are swapped in meaning. areItemsTheSame must answer identity (same id), areContentsTheSame must answer whether visible content is equal. With the buggy pair, a changed order fails identity so the item animator removes and adds it (flicker, jump), and an unchanged-id but changed-content item would be considered same content and never rebind.
  6. Fix:
override fun areItemsTheSame(a: Order, b: Order) = a.id == b.id
override fun areContentsTheSame(a: Order, b: Order) = a == b
override fun getChangePayload(a: Order, b: Order) = if (a.status != b.status) StatusChanged else null

Bind partial updates via payload to get the cross-fade DefaultItemAnimator for changes. 7. Prevention: Unit tests for every ItemCallback; code review checklist. 8. Trade-offs: data class == compares all fields, so keep UI-irrelevant fields out; I would NOT use notifyDataSetChanged (loses animations and state).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Large lists diff cost? → DiffUtil is O(N+D^2) worst case; ListAdapter diffs off-main via AsyncListDiffer.
  • Stable ids vs DiffUtil? → Different tools; with ListAdapter you usually don't need stable ids.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A swapped pair of callbacks shipped because the test used a single-item list.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables animations/notifyDataSetChanged.
  • Hire: corrects the callbacks.
  • Strong hire: explains animator behavior, payloads, and adds tests.

questions.promptHtml: Your Compose screen is janky in a debug build. A teammate says "ship it, release will be fine". How do you decide, and what exactly differs between debug and release for Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can trust or distrust a measurement, and know what R8, baseline profiles and the runtime do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I never judge Compose performance from a debug build. Debug is not optimized by R8, has no baseline profile applied in practice, runs more of the code in the interpreter/JIT, and the app may have debug-only tooling on. I measure a release-like build (R8 on, debuggable false, profileable) with Macrobenchmark and JankStats. If it is still janky there, it's a real problem; if only debug, I deprioritise it but still check the structure (counts, unstable params).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Code execution: on first run, code is interpreted, then JIT-ed, and AOT only through install-time/dex-opt and baseline profiles. Compose is large library code; without a profile, first scroll/navigation executes cold code paths, producing first-frame jank. Compose ships a default profile, but the official guidance still recommends an app-specific one (verify per AGP/Compose version).
  • R8: shrinking, optimization and (in recent AGP) full mode inline small functions, remove unused code; Compose's many tiny functions benefit.
  • Debug overhead: debuggable apps cost more (assertions, no optimizations in some paths).
  • What does NOT differ: recomposition logic. Counts, stability and phase reads are structurally the same, so a screen recomposing 60x per scroll is a bug in both.
Question: slow in debug only?
  yes -> release + R8 + profileable, Macrobenchmark (CompilationMode.None vs Partial)
         still slow -> real problem: counts, compiler report, trace
         fine       -> add baseline profile, do not over-optimize

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Macrobenchmark: compare cold JIT with baseline profile
@Test fun scrollFeed() = rule.measureRepeated(
    packageName = "com.example", metrics = listOf(FrameTimingMetric()),
    compilationMode = CompilationMode.Partial(), iterations = 10,
    startupMode = StartupMode.WARM
) { startActivityAndWait(); device.findObject(By.res("feed")).fling(Direction.DOWN) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking with debuggable true or on an emulator.
  • Declaring a debug problem "fixed" without release verification.
  • Dismissing structural problems because "release is fast on my Pixel".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does CompilationMode.None vs Partial tell you? → None approximates a fresh install without profile; Partial applies baseline profile, so the delta is what the profile buys.
  2. Why test on a low-end device? → Frame budget and CPU headroom shrink; jank appears only there.
  3. Does R8 obfuscation affect Compose? → Needs correct keep rules for reflection/serialization, not for Compose itself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "release is faster". Senior: states the mechanisms (JIT/AOT, profile, R8), separates structural from environmental cost, and quantifies with Macrobenchmark percentiles.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped a cart screen that looked bad in debug; field data (JankStats) showed 2% jank, so they instead fixed the real culprit, a cold first scroll, with a baseline profile.

questions.contextHtml: Release build, 3 GB RAM Android 11 devices (35% of users). Field data: the first scroll after opening the feed shows 30% janky frames, subsequent scrolls 3%. Cold start p50 1.9 s. Perfetto first scroll: long inflate/Compose:compose slices, class loading and JIT on main thread. Red herring: someone points to image sizes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and how do you prove it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Simplify the layout" without noticing the cold/warm asymmetry.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a baseline profile shipped, does it cover the feed scroll, which API levels? Is the profile Play-delivered or only local? Is R8 on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for crash; prioritize the profile release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) no or stale baseline profile for the scroll path; (2) heavy first-item composition; (3) eager initialization (DI graph, image loader) on first scroll; (4) images.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark CompilationMode.None vs Partial on the same device; Perfetto for JIT/class-load slices; trace the first-item composition.
  5. Root cause: Code on the scroll path is interpreted/JIT-compiled the first time; Compose's runtime and lazy list machinery are large. Baseline profile pre-compiles it. Cold-vs-warm gap is the signature.
  6. Fix: Short term add a baseline profile generator covering startup plus a feed fling (Baseline Profile Gradle plugin, BaselineProfileRule), ship in release. Long term: refresh profile each release in CI, trim first-item work, contentType, avoid inflating a heavy ComposeView per item.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI comparing against the previous release; track first-scroll jank in field with JankStats.
  8. Trade-offs: Profiles increase APK size slightly and only help Android 7+ with ART (cloud profiles on Play: verify); I would NOT stuff the profile with every screen, official guidance says to cover critical journeys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Profile doesn't help on API 24 devices? → Delivery depends on install path; verify with dumpsys package dexopt.
  • Warm scroll still 3%? → Next target: image decode size and per-item composition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first scroll fell from 30% to 9% janky frames with a profile, while the "simplify layout" sprint had moved it 1 point.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: micro-optimizes layouts.
  • Hire: baseline profile plus benchmark.
  • Strong hire: A/B via compilation modes, delivery verification, CI regression gate.

questions.contextHtml: Upgrade Kotlin 1.9.x to 2.0.21 with the Compose compiler Gradle plugin and Compose BOM bump. After release, crash-free sessions are unchanged, but p95 frame time is +14% on the Home screen, a "Cannot resolve compose compiler 1.5.x" CI break was patched a week earlier, and Layout Inspector shows fewer recompositions on some screens and more on others. A designer notes an animation now stutters. Stability report diff (before/after) shows Product class went from unstable to stable params on skippable composables. Red herring: AGP version changed too.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: how do you attribute the regression and decide rollback?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert everything" or blaming the new compiler without bisecting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the same release (AGP, Compose BOM, Coil, app code)? Did anyone set strong skipping explicitly? Did Macrobenchmark run before/after?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Staged rollout halt; if p95 is within SLO keep, else roll back via previous build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) strong skipping became default (Kotlin 2.0.20+, the Compose compiler plugin): unstable params skip by instance equality and lambdas are memoized, changing recomposition and exposing latent mutation-in-place bugs; (2) K2 compiler plus new runtime changing code layout; (3) BOM-level behavior changes (lazy layout, text); (4) AGP/R8 changes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bisect in separate PRs: compiler only, then BOM, then AGP; compare compiler reports (reportsDestination) per build; Macrobenchmark identical device matrix; read release notes.
  5. Root cause (example): With strong skipping, a composable taking a mutable Cart instance now skips when the same instance is passed, so in-place mutations stop rendering in one screen; another screen's lambda memoization changed recomposition cost. Measure rather than assume.
  6. Fix: Short term, restore behavior where needed (@NonSkippableComposable, or disable via the compiler feature flag for a transition, verify flag name), fix the mutation bug by emitting new instances. Long term: immutable models and stability config.
  7. Prevention: Gate upgrades behind benchmark diffs; commit compiler reports to CI and diff them; upgrade one dimension per PR.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not reverting Kotlin forever (K2, security, tooling), not turning off strong skipping permanently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does strong skipping make @Stable unnecessary? → It reduces its need for skipping, but stable types still compare via equals, unstable via ===.
  • Lambdas capturing unstable values? → Remembered with captures by instance equality.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a compiler bump a screen that used a mutable model stopped updating; the compiler report diff found the exact composable in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reverts everything.
  • Hire: bisects and reads reports.
  • Strong hire: explains strong-skipping semantics, adds upgrade guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
Settings Fragment embeds ComposeView in XML (fragment_settings.xml) and uses ViewBinding. LeakCanary after navigating back from the screen: GC ROOT ... Fragment.mView -> ComposeView -> Composition -> ... SettingsFragment retained, ~4 MB per visit. Play Console shows OOM rate rising from 0.2% to 0.9% after 20+ navigations. Code:

class SettingsFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_settings) {
    private var binding: FragmentSettingsBinding? = null
    override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
        binding = FragmentSettingsBinding.bind(v)
        binding!!.compose.setContent { SettingsScreen() }
    }
}

Red herring: Coil is suspected.
questions.promptHtml: Find and fix the leak.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call System.gc() or null the ComposeView."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Fragment on the back stack (view destroyed, instance alive)? Which ViewCompositionStrategy is set? Any singleton holding callbacks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the strategy and null the binding; hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) binding field not cleared in onDestroyView, holding the view tree; (2) composition not disposed when the Fragment view is destroyed because the default strategy ties disposal to window detach; (3) lambda capturing the Fragment in a long-lived object; (4) Coil.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace path; heap dump to see ComposeView reachable from SettingsFragment.binding; check strategy.
  5. Root cause: A Fragment on the back stack keeps its instance but destroys its view (onDestroyView). Holding binding retains the view hierarchy; additionally, the default strategy (DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool, since Compose UI 1.2) disposes on window detach, which can lag behind the Fragment's view lifecycle in some navigation flows.
  6. Fix:
override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
    binding = FragmentSettingsBinding.bind(v).also {
        it.compose.setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
        it.compose.setContent { SettingsScreen() }
    }
}
override fun onDestroyView() { binding = null; super.onDestroyView() }
  1. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug; lint on _binding pattern; a base fragment enforcing the strategy.
  2. Trade-offs: I would NOT use DisposeOnLifecycleDestroyed(fragment) (uses fragment lifecycle, not view lifecycle) for XML-hosted ComposeViews.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• ComposeView programmatically created in onCreateView? → Same strategy; set it before setContent.
  • Fragment-compose helper? → Newer fragment-compose artifacts offer helpers (verify version).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A back-stack-heavy flow grew heap 80 MB over a session until ComposeView holders were fixed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: nulls things randomly.
  • Hire: strategy plus binding cleanup.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes fragment vs view lifecycle, explains default strategy.

questions.contextHtml:
A "like" heart plus confetti animation on a video feed. Devices: 60 Hz mid-range. During the 1.2 s animation, FeedScreen recomposes ~70 times and frame time rises to 28 ms. Code:

val progress by animateFloatAsState(if (liked) 1f else 0f, tween(1200))
Column {
    Heart(size = (24 + 24 * progress).dp)       // reads progress in composition
    Confetti(progress)
    VideoList(items)                             // unrelated, large
}

Red herring: Lottie file size.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the whole screen recompose and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce duration" or "use remember".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where do progress reads occur? Is FeedScreen or a leaf hosting the animation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shorten/disable confetti via flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) animated State read in composition of a large scope; (2) VideoList not skippable/stable; (3) drawing cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recomposition counts per frame; trace composition slices.
  5. Root cause: by animateFloatAsState reads .value where it is delegated, in the composable body; each frame invalidates that scope. Because the scope includes VideoList, everything re-executes.
  6. Fix: Move the animation into a small composable, and read in draw/layout.
@Composable fun Heart(liked: Boolean) {
    val progress = animateFloatAsState(if (liked) 1f else 0f, tween(1200))
    Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer { val s = 1f + progress.value; scaleX = s; scaleY = s })
}

Passing () -> Float/State<Float> down defers the read. 7. Prevention: Review rule: animated values are consumed via graphicsLayer/drawBehind/offset {} lambdas; benchmark animation frames. 8. Trade-offs: Size changes need layout, so animate via layout lambda or graphicsLayer scale if semantics allow; I would NOT animate Modifier.size directly on a huge subtree.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• AnimatedVisibility vs this? → It animates in the layout/draw phases internally.
  • Animatable vs animateFloatAsState? → Animatable gives imperative control (gestures), same read rules.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single graphicsLayer swap removed 70 recompositions per animation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fiddles with duration.
  • Hire: moves reads into lambdas.
  • Strong hire: names phases and verifies.

questions.contextHtml: Settings screen with 40 rows. Toggling any switch recomposes all 40 rows (counts show 40 per toggle). The project is on Kotlin 1.9.22 with Compose compiler 1.5.8, strong skipping off. Compiler report: restartable but NOT skippable for SettingRow because of settings: List<Setting> (kotlin.collections.List) and onClick: () -> Unit capturing the unstable ViewModel. Team of 12, 60 screens; leadership wants a decision between (A) upgrade to strong skipping, (B) annotate/migrate models, (C) ignore.
questions.promptHtml: Recommend a path with numbers and risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap everything in remember" or annotate all with @Immutable blindly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we move to Kotlin 2.0.20+ soon? How many modules, are models in a non-Compose module (compiler cannot infer)? Is the screen actually slow (frame time) or only counts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For this screen: hoist per-row state, key rows, pass primitive params.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) List is treated unstable; (2) lambdas capturing unstable VM re-allocate each recomposition; (3) model classes in another module lacking stability info.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compose compiler reports/metrics (-composables.txt, -classes.txt); counts before/after.
  5. Root cause: Without strong skipping, a composable with any unstable parameter is not skippable; its caller recomposing re-executes it. Unstable lambdas cannot be compared.
  6. Fix: Recommend (A) as default (strong skipping on Kotlin 2.0.20+: unstable params compare by instance ===, lambdas auto-remembered), plus (B) targeted: immutable collections or stability config file for known-immutable external types, and fix places mutating in place since instance equality skips them.
  7. Prevention: Report diff in CI; guideline: ImmutableList/value classes in UI models.
  8. Trade-offs: Strong skipping is not free: composables skip when same instance even if mutated (bug source), and unstable types equal per equals only if stable; I would NOT annotate @Immutable on classes holding mutable fields (a lie breaks correctness).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why 40 rows recompose on one toggle? → The parent reads the whole list state; rows with changed params recompose, others skipped only if skippable.
  • What does @Stable promise? → Equality is consistent and changes notify composition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Upgrading and mapping List<T> through a stability config dropped recomposition counts by ~95% on three big screens, but exposed two mutate-in-place bugs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random annotations.
  • Hire: strong skipping plus reports.
  • Strong hire: weighs risks (identity-skip bugs), rollout and CI gating.

questions.contextHtml:
A home screen shows a vertically scrolling list of carousels. Crash in production after a QA change: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Vertically scrollable component was measured with an infinity maximum height constraints. The earlier version worked but janked: opening Home composes 12 carousels x 20 items = 240 items. Code now:

Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())) {
    sections.forEach { s ->
        Text(s.title)
        LazyColumn { items(s.items) { Card(it) } }      // nested vertical lazy list
    }
}

Also horizontal scroll position of each carousel resets on returning from detail. Red herring: "Compose lists are always slow".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the crash and redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Sets a fixed height on the inner list.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are inner lists vertical or horizontal? Item counts? Do we need sticky headers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert to previous version or change inner lists to non-lazy Column for small counts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) lazy list measured in an infinite-height scrollable parent; (2) carousel state not saved (no stable key per section); (3) subcomposition of everything at once.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stack trace; counts; Layout Inspector.
  5. Root cause: Lazy layouts need bounded constraints in the scroll direction; verticalScroll gives infinity. Also a lazy list inside a non-lazy scroll parent composes all content (defeating laziness).
  6. Fix: One outer LazyColumn, sections as items, inner LazyRow for horizontal carousels with state per section.
LazyColumn {
    items(sections, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "carousel" }) { s ->
        Text(s.title)
        val rowState = rememberLazyListState()   // saved via the item key
        LazyRow(state = rowState) { items(s.items, key = { it.id }) { Card(it) } }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/review; Macrobenchmark on Home.
  2. Trade-offs: rememberLazyListState inside an item lives as long as the item is composed; for restoration across disposal use rememberSaveable(s.id) with LazyListState.Saver (it is saveable by default but keyed by position in the slot table, so use key). I would NOT set fixed heights.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Nested scrolling in the same direction? → Disallowed; use flattened items.
  • Why does key help with inner state? → Inner state identity follows the item key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "fixed height inner list" workaround clipped content on tablets and was removed later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixed height hack.
  • Hire: flatten with a single outer lazy list.
  • Strong hire: explains constraints, state keys, prefetch for inner rows.

questions.contextHtml: A 40-screen View-based app (Fragments, Navigation component, XML, ViewBinding), 5M MAU, crash-free 99.7%, a team of 14, 3 quarters of runway. Product still ships features every sprint. Leadership asks "migrate to Compose". Concerns: APK size (+~2 MB), cold start, hiring, the custom design-system views. Red herring: someone proposes a big-bang rewrite branch.
questions.promptHtml: Present the migration plan, sequencing and guardrails.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite screen by screen over the weekend" or a big-bang branch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the driver (velocity, design system, hiring)? Test coverage per screen? Which screens change most? Multi-module?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; first make the app Compose-ready: enable Compose, set up theme interop (Material 3 theme adapting XML themes), CI with benchmarks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (1) startup/size regressions; (2) state duplication at View/Compose boundaries; (3) navigation split-brain; (4) inconsistent design.
  4. How I'd verify each: Baseline Macrobenchmarks for startup and top-5 journeys before touching anything; track APK/R8 size; JankStats field metrics.
  5. Root cause of failure modes: big-bang migrations stall features and hide regressions.
  6. Plan: (a) Build a Compose design system with tokens that mirror XML themes. (b) Start with new screens and leaf components via ComposeView in Fragments (set DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed). (c) Migrate lowest-risk, highest-churn screens next; keep complex RecyclerView-heavy screens for later (or LazyColumn with a feature flag). (d) Navigation: keep Fragment navigation until >70% screens are Compose, then move to Navigation Compose or keep a single-activity with fragment-compose interop. (e) Shared state through ViewModels (UDF), not through View state. (f) Delete XML per screen when done; track a migration burn-down.
  7. Prevention: Guardrails: benchmark gate per PR touching migrated screens, screenshot tests, a11y checks, feature flags with staged rollouts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not big-bang; not migrating stable low-churn screens just for purity; not mixing two navigation systems indefinitely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Startup regression? → Baseline profile covering Compose; measure with CompilationMode comparisons.
  • Embedding existing custom Views? → AndroidView with an update lambda; plan to rewrite hot ones.
  • RecyclerView inside Compose or vice versa? → ComposeView item is OK for few items; avoid heavy per-row ComposeViews at scale (see Q379).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team migrated detail screens first because they had low risk and found the toolbars/theme gap was the real work.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big bang.
  • Hire: incremental with interop.
  • Strong hire: metrics baseline, nav strategy, guardrails, burn-down and rollback.

questions.contextHtml: Two weeks before a banking-app launch the accessibility audit (TalkBack + Accessibility Scanner) fails the Compose onboarding and a View-based payments screen. Findings: icon-only buttons announced as "Button"; a custom toggle row reads "On" with no label; touch targets 32 dp; low contrast #9E9E9E on white (2.7:1); font scale 200% truncates text; each product card reads as 6 separate focus stops; the error text is not announced. The PM says "just add contentDescription everywhere".
questions.promptHtml: How do you triage and fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blanket contentDescription including on decorative images, ignoring merging and focus order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Target standard (WCAG 2.1 AA?), languages, which TalkBack versions? Is launch-blocking severity defined?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix blockers first: unlabeled actions, targets, contrast, announcements.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing semantics, over-fragmented semantics tree, size/contrast tokens, no live region.
  4. How I'd verify each: TalkBack manual run, Accessibility Scanner, semantics tests (onNodeWithContentDescription, assertHasClickAction), font scale 2.0, Compose Modifier.semantics inspection in Layout Inspector.
  5. Root cause: Components built from raw Box/Icon lacking semantics; no design tokens for min target and contrast.
  6. Fix:
IconButton(onClick = onClose) { Icon(Icons.Default.Close, contentDescription = stringResource(R.string.close)) } // 48dp min touch target
Row(Modifier.toggleable(value = on, role = Role.Switch, onValueChange = onChange)
      .semantics { stateDescription = if (on) "Enabled" else "Disabled" }) { Text(label); Switch(on, null) }
Card(Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {}) { /* merged into one stop */ }
Text(err, Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite })

Decorative images use contentDescription = null. Views: android:labelFor, importantForAccessibility, ViewCompat.setAccessibilityDelegate. 7. Prevention: Design-system defaults (48 dp, contrast checks), CI scanner, semantics tests, QA TalkBack checklist. 8. Trade-offs: I would NOT put descriptions on every node, nor suppress content to pass the scanner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Text truncation at 200%? → Let containers grow, use sp, avoid fixed heights.
  • RTL? → Use start/end, test mirrored icons.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Merging card semantics reduced a screen from ~60 focus stops to ~12, which testers said was the real improvement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: contentDescription everywhere.
  • Hire: labels, roles, targets, contrast.
  • Strong hire: merging, live regions, font scale, tests, tokens.

questions.subtopic: Edge-to-edge, insets and IME on tablets
questions.contextHtml: After raising targetSdk to 35, tablet users (10-inch, Android 15) report: the top bar overlaps the status bar, the bottom nav sits under the gesture bar, and in the login form the keyboard covers the Submit button. Phones show double padding at the bottom with the keyboard open on Android 10 devices. Code: enableEdgeToEdge() is called, theme sets windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize", and each screen applies Modifier.imePadding() plus the Scaffold inner padding. Ratings dropped from 4.6 to 4.3 in a week.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix across phones, tablets and old API levels.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: android:fitsSystemWindows="true" everywhere or setting setDecorFitsSystemWindows(true) (no longer opts out on Android 15).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens, which API levels, gesture vs 3-button nav, any custom top bars?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the login screen padding; roll out gradually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Insets consumed twice or not applied (custom bars ignore WindowInsets.safeDrawing); (2) adjustResize combined with enableEdgeToEdge double-applies IME inset on older APIs; (3) tablet taskbar/caption insets differ; (4) Scaffold padding ignored.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector insets, emulator with resizable/tablet AVD, Android 10 AVD, test with taskbar and gesture nav.
  5. Root cause: Targeting 35 enforces edge-to-edge on Android 15+, so each screen must handle insets; mixing adjustResize with manual IME handling doubles padding on API < 30.
  6. Fix: Remove adjustResize reliance, handle insets in one place.
Scaffold(
  topBar = { TopAppBar(title = { Text("Login") }) },    // M3 bars apply status bar insets
  contentWindowInsets = WindowInsets.safeDrawing
) { padding ->
    Column(Modifier.padding(padding).consumeWindowInsets(padding).imePadding().verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())) { /* form */ }
}

Use consumeWindowInsets so imePadding does not double up; a NavigationBar handles bottom insets itself. 7. Prevention: Insets in the design system; screenshot tests with DeviceConfigurationOverride; test matrix: API 29/34/35, gesture and 3-button, tablet. 8. Trade-offs: I would NOT revert targetSdk (Play policy), nor pad with magic dp values.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-window/freeform? → Insets change dynamically; avoid cached values.
  • Display cutouts landscape? → WindowInsets.displayCutout is part of safeDrawing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hardcoded 24 dp top padding looked fine on phones and overlapped on tablets with taskbars.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fitsSystemWindows hacks.
  • Hire: consistent inset handling.
  • Strong hire: consume semantics, API matrix, tests and rollout.

questions.promptHtml: A screen is janky. Walk me through how you decide whether the problem is in composition, layout, draw, the RenderThread/GPU, or something outside UI entirely, and which tool you use at each step.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior must triage across Compose, Views and rendering rather than apply a favorite fix.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I first confirm the jank in a release-like build with frame timing, then use a system trace to see where the missed frames spend time: UI thread slices (Compose:recompose, measure/layout, Choreographer#doFrame), RenderThread (DrawFrames, texture upload) or GPU. UI thread long means composition/layout/inflation; RenderThread long means drawing/overdraw/bitmaps/shaders; main-thread blocking means I/O, locks, GC.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per frame budget: 16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz (1000/60, 1000/120).

VSYNC -> UI thread: input -> animation -> composition -> layout -> draw (record display list)
      -> RenderThread: sync, execute display list, GPU -> SurfaceFlinger -> display
Missed deadline = UI thread time + RenderThread time > budget (or pipeline stall)

Decision tree:

  • JankStats/FrameTimingMetric shows slow frames: where in a trace?
  • Long Compose:recompose or many recompositions: state read too high, unstable params, heavy work in composition.
  • Long measure/layout: nested intrinsics, subcompose layouts, deep trees.
  • Long draw/DrawFrame on RenderThread: overdraw, large bitmaps, complex clip, shader compile (first-use).
  • GC or Lock contention slices on main: allocation churn in composition.
  • Only first scroll slow: JIT/baseline profile. Tools: Perfetto/System Trace, Layout Inspector, compiler reports, GPU profiler, dumpsys gfxinfo, FrameMetrics, Macrobenchmark.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Custom trace section for attribution
Trace.beginSection("ProductMapping"); try { map() } finally { Trace.endSection() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Optimizing recomposition when the RenderThread is the long pole.
  • Using debug traces.
  • Ignoring buffer stuffing/pipeline issues.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the UI thread is idle but frames are late? → RenderThread/GPU or SurfaceFlinger; check frame timeline.
  2. Only on one device class? → GPU/driver/refresh rate; compare traces.
  3. How do you attribute in field? → JankStats with state tags, plus FrameMetrics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE guesses "recomposition". Senior has a decision tree, uses the frame budget math, and proves the cause with a trace.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent days on recomposition; the trace showed a 4096x4096 bitmap upload on the RenderThread.

questions.contextHtml: JankStats field data: jank rate 3% overall but 22% on one family of 120 Hz mid-range devices (about 8% of DAU) running Android 13; the same screen is smooth on Pixel 7. Perfetto from a lab device: UI thread frames ~6 ms (fine), RenderThread DrawFrames ~10 ms, flush commands slices large; gradient-blurred card backgrounds (Modifier.blur, shadows) cover the screen. Red herring: GC.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it without dropping the design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce recomposition" (UI thread is fine).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which GPU, refresh rate, resolution? Does the jank follow animation or static scroll?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag expensive effects by device class (low-RAM/GPU) via remote config.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) GPU fill-rate/overdraw from blur and shadows at 120 Hz budget 8.3 ms; (2) large textures; (3) shader compile on first draw; (4) display mode switching.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto frame timeline (GPU slices), dumpsys gfxinfo histogram, Profile GPU rendering, Android GPU Inspector (verify availability for the device), overdraw visualization.
  5. Root cause: Budget halves at 120 Hz (8.3 ms) and the device's GPU needs ~10 ms per frame for blur/shadows; UI work is not the bottleneck.
  6. Fix: Short term disable/downgrade blur on that class, replace shadows with elevation tokens or pre-rendered assets, flatten overlapping opaque layers. Long term: design-system tokens for effect tiers, graphicsLayer caching for static content (CompositingStrategy.Offscreen only when required).
  7. Prevention: Device lab including mid-range 120 Hz devices, Macrobenchmark on them, performance budget.
  8. Trade-offs: Not capping refresh rate globally; I would NOT drop the feature without a fallback.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Blur support? → Modifier.blur is only effective on Android 12+ (RenderEffect); verify fallback.
  • Why does it appear on 120 Hz only? → Same work, half the time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A glassmorphism redesign was perfect on flagship phones and unusable on mid-range ones until an effect tier was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames recomposition.
  • Hire: identifies RenderThread/GPU.
  • Strong hire: budget math, tiering, device lab.

questions.contextHtml:
A "scroll to top" button should appear when the list is scrolled past the first item. After a change, the whole screen recomposes on every scroll frame. Code:

val listState = rememberLazyListState()
val showButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0   // plain read
Box { LazyColumn(state = listState) { ... }
      if (showButton) ScrollToTop() }

Red herring: LazyColumn items count.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what is the fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use remember(listState)" which does not help.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the update frequency of the underlying state and how often does the derived output change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None, minor.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) reading a fast-changing state in composition; (2) list items not skippable.
  4. How I'd verify each: Recomposition counts during scroll.
  5. Root cause: firstVisibleItemIndex changes whenever the first item changes, and the read is in the parent scope, so the scope recomposes on every change though the Boolean output changes rarely.
  6. Fix:
val showButton by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }

The composable now only invalidates when the derived result changes. 7. Prevention: Review: boolean/threshold from a fast input uses derivedStateOf. 8. Trade-offs: derivedStateOf has overhead; I would NOT use it when output changes as often as input (e.g. alpha tied to offset; use a lambda/layer read instead).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does it need remember? → Yes, otherwise a new derived state each recomposition.
  • Alternative? → snapshotFlow for side effects.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single derivedStateOf removed per-frame recomposition of a long screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: remember misuse.
  • Hire: derivedStateOf.
  • Strong hire: explains when it does not help.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders screen with 5,000 rows for B2B users (3% of DAU). ANR rate on this screen: 1.4%, Play vitals threshold is 0.47% (verify current user-perceived bad behavior threshold). Stack: main blocked in kotlin.collections.CollectionsKt.sortedWith ← OrdersScreen ← Recomposer. Code:

@Composable
fun OrdersScreen(orders: List<Order>, query: String) {
    val visible = orders.filter { it.matches(query) }.sortedByDescending { it.date }   // every recomposition
    LazyColumn { items(visible, key = { it.id }) { OrderRow(it) } }
}

query changes on every keystroke. Red herring: OrderRow is expensive.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the ANR and propose the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps in remember without keys or moves to LaunchedEffect with mutable list state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does orders come from? Does the data change often? Is full sort needed on device?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap results or pre-sort on the server in a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) O(n log n) sort + filter in composition on the main thread each recomposition; (2) filter by regex; (3) row cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace slice for composition; ANR traces on Play; Trace sections.
  5. Root cause: Composition runs on the main thread; 5,000 items filtered and sorted per keystroke cost tens of ms and stack under typing, blowing the frame and input budget until ANR.
  6. Fix: Move derivation to the ViewModel/domain layer with Flow, off-main; or in UI with remember(orders, query) as an interim.
val visible = remember(orders, query) { orders.filter { it.matches(query) }.sortedByDescending { it.date } } // interim
// long term: vm.visible = combine(orders, query.debounce(150)) { ... }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default).stateIn(...)
  1. Prevention: StrictMode, trace budget alarms, lint "no collection ops in composables".
  2. Trade-offs: remember still computes on main on first run; I would NOT use produceState with unbounded work without cancellation; consider paging.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• derivedStateOf here? → For state reads only; the cost is the computation, move it off-main.
  • Do items need key? → Yes for stable identity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tiny" sort in a composable passed review because test data had 20 rows.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames rows.
  • Hire: moves/caches the computation.
  • Strong hire: off-main with Flow, benchmark with production-sized data.

questions.contextHtml: A photo grid (3 columns, ~600 items) on 3 GB devices. Crash reports: OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 33177616 byte allocation (a 4608x1800-ish bitmap) on ~0.8% of sessions; scroll shows hitches when new rows appear. Thumbnails come from a 12 MP originals CDN path. Code uses AsyncImage(model = url, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()) with ContentScale.Crop. Red herring: the grid library.
questions.promptHtml: Why the OOM and hitches, and how do you fix and verify?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap with largeHeap" or "use Glide".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the cell size in px? Is the loader downsampling to the target size? Is there a memory cache cap? Does the server provide thumbnails?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Request smaller server renditions; lower the loader's memory cache size.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) full-resolution decode (width x height x 4 bytes ARGB_8888; 33,177,616 B is about 31.6 MB per bitmap); (2) size resolved as unbounded because the modifier has no constraint at request time; (3) texture upload on RenderThread causing hitches; (4) too many items cached.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump/Memory Profiler for bitmap sizes; trace for texture upload; loader debug logs for requested size.
  5. Root cause: Decoding a large bitmap per cell when a ~360x360 px cell needs ~0.5 MB (360 x 360 x 4 = 518,400 B). Full-size bitmaps also stall texture upload.
  6. Fix: Use a loader that sizes to layout (Coil's AsyncImage resolves size from constraints; ensure the cell has bounded size via aspectRatio and fixed grid cell width), request CDN thumbnails at cell px, use Bitmap.Config.RGB_565 only if acceptable, set memory cache percent, contentType and keys on the grid, placeholders with fixed size.
LazyVerticalGrid(GridCells.Fixed(3)) {
    items(photos, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "photo" }) { p ->
        AsyncImage(model = ImageRequest.Builder(ctx).data(p.thumbUrl(px = 360)).crossfade(true).build(),
            contentDescription = null, contentScale = ContentScale.Crop,
            modifier = Modifier.aspectRatio(1f))
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Memory budget tests, Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric, bitmap-size lint in review.
  2. Trade-offs: Hardware bitmaps save heap but cannot be read back; I would NOT use largeHeap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Calculating bitmap memory? → w x h x bytes/pixel (4 for ARGB_8888).
  • Still hitching with small bitmaps? → Check decode off-main, prefetch, per-item composition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A CDN param change from w=1080 to w=360 took OOMs from 0.8% to under 0.1%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: largeHeap.
  • Hire: downsample to target.
  • Strong hire: math, caches, server renditions, verification.

questions.contextHtml:
During a partial migration, each RecyclerView row (feed of 200 items) is a ComposeView holder. Fast fling on mid-range devices drops to ~35 fps; memory climbs 40 MB; sometimes rows show a previous item's content. Trace: long Choreographer#doFrame with createViewHolder -> ComposeView.setContent each time. Code:

class Holder(val cv: ComposeView) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(cv) {
    fun bind(item: Item) { cv.setContent { ItemRow(item) } }
}

Red herring: "Compose is slow".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose in RecyclerView is not supported."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which ViewCompositionStrategy? Is the pool shared? Heterogeneous row types?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the heaviest row types to Views.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) a new composition created on every bind (setContent per bind); (2) default strategy ties disposal to window detach, so recycled holders keep compositions; (3) no RecycledViewPool tuning; (4) stale content from captured item.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace slices for setContent/composition; heap dump count of Composition.
  5. Root cause: Calling setContent per bind rebuilds the composition; the correct pattern is to set content once and update state.
  6. Fix: Set content once in the holder, drive it with state; use DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed or the pool-aware default (DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool, Compose UI 1.2+).
class Holder(val cv: ComposeView) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(cv) {
    private val item = mutableStateOf<Item?>(null)
    init { cv.setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
           cv.setContent { item.value?.let { ItemRow(it) } } }
    fun bind(i: Item) { item.value = i }
}

Long term migrate the whole list to LazyColumn with keys. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark for the screen; guidelines. 8. Trade-offs: Each ComposeView carries composition overhead; I would NOT mix per-row ComposeViews across big lists permanently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not remember the content? → The ComposeView is reused; remembered state lives in its composition.
  • Pool? → Share RecycledViewPool, size it per type.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Setting content once removed ~12 ms per row creation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: unsupported claim.
  • Hire: set content once with state.
  • Strong hire: lifecycle strategy, trade-offs, migration path.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a custom stock-style chart with 5,000 points, pinch-to-zoom, crosshair tooltip and a11y support, on an app with both Compose and Views screens. The requirement says "must be smooth on low-end devices". Options: a custom View, Compose Canvas, or a third-party library.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and why? What do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose, because it's modern."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens host it, min API, update frequency (streaming?), a11y requirements, existing libs license?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; prototype both and measure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Canvas is fine for static or low-frequency updates; a custom View/SurfaceView better for high-frequency streaming; library for speed to market.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark on a low-end device with 5,000 points, trace draw time.
  5. Root cause of decision: Cost per frame: path drawing of 5,000 points is a single drawPath if you build a Path once and avoid per-frame allocation.
  6. Fix/decision: Compose Canvas with drawWithCache, gestures in pointerInput/transformable read in the draw phase (state in lambdas), decimate points to pixel width, expose semantics for summary. Fall back to a custom View if streaming needs SurfaceView.
Canvas(Modifier.fillMaxSize().pointerInput(Unit) { detectTransformGestures { _, pan, zoom, _ -> vm.onTransform(pan, zoom) } }) {
    drawPath(path = pathFor(viewport()), color = line, style = Stroke(2.dp.toPx()))
}
  1. Prevention: Benchmarks and a11y tests.
  2. Trade-offs: Third-party library speeds delivery but limits custom a11y; I would NOT hand-roll unless needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tooltips reading state? → Read in draw phase.
  • 50k points? → Decimate (min/max per pixel column).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Decimating to pixel columns cut draw from ~14 ms to ~2 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fashion choice.
  • Hire: measured choice.
  • Strong hire: phases, decimation, a11y, fallback.

questions.contextHtml: Crash spike after release: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1,048,xxx bytes when users background the app on the Gallery screen (0.6% of sessions), plus BadParcelableException/IllegalArgumentException: ... cannot be saved using the current SaveableStateRegistry in debug. Change: per-item rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(photo) } where Photo is a non-Parcelable class holding a 1.5 MB thumbnail, in a list of 300 items.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What goes into saved state? Which Android versions? Is the data re-fetchable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix removing large saves; staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Bundle size exceeded binder transaction limit (about 1 MB shared across the process); (2) non-saveable type; (3) per-item saves multiply.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log bundle size (Parcel.dataSize), Android Studio's saved state inspection, repro by backgrounding.
  5. Root cause: rememberSaveable writes into the Activity's saved-instance-state Bundle, which is transported via Binder on stop with a ~1 MB process-wide limit. Large objects and per-item copies blow it.
  6. Fix: Save only identifiers and small UI state (selected id, scroll position, ~bytes); keep data in a repository/Room; use SavedStateHandle in the ViewModel for small state.
var selectedId by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf<Long?>(null) }   // small and Bundle-safe
  1. Prevention: Guideline: saved state under tens of KB; test with "Don't keep activities" and process-death; lint/review.
  2. Trade-offs: Persisting to disk for heavy state; I would NOT increase limits (not possible) or catch exceptions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Custom types? → Saver/mapSaver/@Parcelize.
  • Process death vs config change? → ViewModel survives only config change; see A2.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "restore everything" requirement ended as saving three ids.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catches exception.
  • Hire: ids only.
  • Strong hire: limits, testing, storage choices.

questions.contextHtml: A live-event chat screen handled 2 messages/s. The event grows 10x: 20 messages/s, 5,000+ messages in memory, auto-scroll to bottom, reactions animating. p95 frame time 30 ms; main-thread allocations spike; log: Background concurrent copying GC freed ... paused 8ms. Code: val messages = remember { mutableStateListOf<Message>() } appended from a socket thread; LazyColumn without keys; each item reads LocalContext.current and formats time with SimpleDateFormat per recomposition.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign for 10x.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a debounce" only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the user pinned to bottom or reading history? Is every message needed on screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap retained messages (e.g. 500) and batch updates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) writes from a background thread into a snapshot state list and per-message state changes; (2) no keys so insertions shift identity; (3) per-item allocations (formatters); (4) animations per reaction recomposing the screen.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace, allocation profiler, counts.
  5. Root cause: Unbatched mutations produce many snapshot applies and recompositions per second; allocations create GC pressure.
  6. Fix: Buffer socket events in the data layer and emit batches (e.g. 100 ms window) to an immutable StateFlow<List<Message>>; LazyColumn with key/contentType, reverseLayout = true; preformat time in the model mapper; scroll-to-bottom only when pinned, using derivedStateOf on listState.canScrollForward; reaction animations in graphicsLayer.
val atBottom by remember { derivedStateOf { !listState.canScrollForward } }
LaunchedEffect(messages.size) { if (atBottom) listState.animateScrollToItem(0) }   // reverseLayout
  1. Prevention: Load test with synthetic feed; Macrobenchmark.
  2. Trade-offs: Batching adds up to 100 ms display delay; I would NOT animate every scroll, use scrollToItem under heavy rates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory? → Windowed list, discard old.
  • Out-of-order messages? → Sort by server id at the mapper.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to 100 ms batching removed jank with no user-visible lag.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debounce only.
  • Hire: batching and keys.
  • Strong hire: pinned-scroll logic, allocation fixes, load testing.

questions.promptHtml: How do you stop UI performance regressions from reaching production on a team of 20 Android engineers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors build systems, not heroics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I define budgets (startup time, jank %, frame percentiles) per key journey, measure them in CI with Macrobenchmark on a fixed low-end device, compare against the baseline of the previous release, and block merges on regression beyond a threshold. In production I track JankStats and Play vitals with alerts, and guard code-level causes with compiler report diffs and lint.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers:

PR:      lint + compiler reports diff + unit/semantic tests
Nightly: Macrobenchmark (startup, scroll) on device farm -> trend dashboard
Release: staged rollout, JankStats / Play vitals watch, auto-halt on thresholds

Details: stable test devices (thermal state, battery, no emulators), enough iterations (e.g. 10+, use medians and p90, verify variance), baseline profile regenerated per release, compare CompilationMode.Partial against previous artifacts, alert on p95 frame duration and ANR.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@get:Rule val rule = MacrobenchmarkRule()
@Test fun feedScroll() = rule.measureRepeated(packageName = "com.example",
    metrics = listOf(FrameTimingMetric()), iterations = 10, startupMode = StartupMode.WARM,
    compilationMode = CompilationMode.Partial()) { startActivityAndWait(); device.findObject(By.res("feed")).fling(Direction.DOWN) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running benchmarks on emulators or a single noisy run.
  • Alerting on averages.
  • No ownership for fixing regressions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Flaky benchmarks? → Fixed device, locked clocks if possible, more iterations, compare relative deltas.
  2. What to block on? → Regressions beyond noise, e.g. >10% p95 (tune per data).
  3. Field vs lab? → Lab for gating, field for truth; JankStats with state tags.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "profile before release". Senior: automated gates, budgets, ownership, and rollout controls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library bump added 6 ms per frame; a nightly benchmark caught it before release.

questions.contextHtml: The main feed (RecyclerView, ListAdapter, 6 view types, 8M MAU, 99.8% crash-free) is being rewritten as LazyColumn. Constraints: no regression in scroll jank (currently 2.1%), ad impressions are tracked per item visibility, deep-link scroll positions must work, and the team wants a 4-week staged rollout. Red herring: "LazyColumn is always faster".
questions.promptHtml: How do you ship it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Flip the flag for everyone after QA.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Impression semantics (50% visible for 1 s)? Min API/device mix? Analytics ownership? Rollback ability?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config kill switch retaining the RecyclerView path for the whole rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (1) impression tracking differs (item composition is not visibility); (2) scroll position restoration; (3) jank on low-end; (4) item animation/prefetch differences.
  4. How I'd verify each: A/B with JankStats, impression parity comparisons, Macrobenchmark parity.
  5. Plan: Shared presentation layer (same list models, UDF state). New list: key, contentType per type, LazyListState restoration, impressions via snapshotFlow on layoutInfo.visibleItemsInfo with thresholds; baseline profile; stable models.
  6. Rollout: 1% internal, 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, with auto-halt on jank/ANR/crash/impression deltas.
  7. Prevention: Benchmarks, parity tests, dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs: Keeping two implementations for 4 weeks costs maintenance; I would NOT migrate ad logic and the list simultaneously.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Impressions differ by 6%? → Compare definitions; fix before widening.
  • Low-end jank worse? → Pause rollout for that class, investigate with traces.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Impression drift was the blocker, not performance.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flip flag for all.
  • Hire: flagged staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: metric parity, auto-halt, separate risky changes.
